headline: Vermont sets Oct. 26 start for $31.7M farm and timber recovery program
dek: The state program will reimburse up to 95% of eligible unmet losses from qualifying 2023 and 2024 weather events, with first-phase payments capped at $75,000.
body: Vermont will begin accepting applications Oct. 26 for a $31.7 million disaster-assistance program aimed at farms, forest landowners and logging contractors still recovering from qualifying weather-related losses in 2023 and 2024. The first phase will reimburse up to 95% of eligible unmet losses, with a maximum payment of $75,000, according to the [Office of Gov. Phil Scott](https://governor.vermont.gov/press-release/governor-phil-scott-announces-317-million-vermont-agriculture-timber-disaster).

The Vermont Agriculture and Timber Disaster Assistance Program is designed for businesses that were operating in one of those two years, experienced a qualifying weather loss and are still operating now. Applications are expected to remain open through Dec. 31, and the state anticipates distributing payments in early 2027. The program is noncompetitive: applicants who document eligible unmet losses are to receive a payment, rather than competing for a limited pool of scored awards.

The assistance is broad enough to reach several parts of a farm operation. The state says eligible agricultural losses may include damage to on-farm infrastructure, bare-ground practices, future economic loss and market loss. In a report on the launch, [WCAX](https://www.wcax.com/2026/09/30/vermont-launches-31m-flood-recovery-fund-farmers-foresters/) described the program as a way to help agricultural and forestry businesses catch up on costs connected to flooding and recovery. That framing matters because the qualifying events are in the past; the program is intended to cover documented losses that may already have been repaired, rebuilt or replanted as well as approved work that has not yet been completed.

Timber applicants face a different documentation burden. The [Vermont Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation](https://fpr.vermont.gov/forests/watershed-forestry/vermont-timber-disaster-assistance-program) says the program can cover standing-timber losses, harvested-timber losses, some costs of reopening damaged harvest sites and certain forest-management-plan updates. Applicants should be prepared to provide proof of ownership or financial interest, stand maps, photos, a description of the weather damage and, where required, a licensed-forester assessment. Public agencies and government organizations are not eligible for the timber component.

The state is asking potential applicants to begin assembling records before the portal opens. The governor’s announcement lists ownership or lease documents, parcel information, tax or business identification, time-stamped photographs, receipts or repair estimates and records of other payments received for the same loss. Those requirements are intended to prevent duplicate recovery payments, which means an applicant’s award may depend as much on the paper trail as on the original damage.

The money comes from a federal block grant authorized under the American Relief Act of 2025. Vermont announced the $31.7 million allocation in June, and [VTDigger](https://vtdigger.org/2026/06/10/feds-approve-31-7-million-in-disaster-aid-for-flood-hit-vermont-farmers/) reported at the time that the funding was aimed in part at farmers with limited access to other federal disaster programs. The September rollout supplies the application date and operating rules that were not yet settled in that earlier announcement.

A second phase will address larger infrastructure losses. The state says projects valued above $75,000, up to a $750,000 maximum, will be handled through a competitive grant program. Receiving a first-phase payment will not automatically disqualify an applicant from the second phase, but the same loss cannot be paid twice. Vermont has not yet published the second-phase application schedule, so the immediate deadline for farms and forest businesses is the Dec. 31 first-phase cutoff.

For producers, landowners and loggers, the next step is preparation rather than immediate submission: identify the weather event, separate losses already covered by another program, gather dated evidence and check the state’s agriculture or forestry guidance as the portal launch approaches. Vermont officials say additional application instructions and assistance will be released before Oct. 26.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Vermont farm and timber disaster aid opens Oct. 26
seoDescription: Vermont's $31.7 million farm and timber disaster program opens Oct. 26 for qualifying 2023 and 2024 weather losses.
